title: The Right to Bear Arms
hook: How does a court decide which weapons are protected? The U.S. Supreme Court's answer turns on a deceptively simple phrase: arms 'in common use.'
key_points: The Second Amendment ties 'the right of the people to keep and bear Arms' to a 'well regulated Militia' — and courts long debated whether it was an individual right.
District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) held it protects an individual right to keep common arms for lawful purposes like self-defense at home.
To decide what counts as a protected 'arm,' courts ask if it is a 'bearable arm' and whether it is 'in common use' by law-abiding people.
The right is not unlimited: 'dangerous and unusual' weapons, and arms designed mainly for military use, can fall outside it.
Big questions stay unsettled — notably whether bans on semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines are constitutional.
content_html: The Second Amendment is a single sentence, yet few clauses in the U.S. Constitution have produced more argument. It reads that "a well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed" — and for much of American history courts read it narrowly, as a protection tied to militia service rather than a personal right.
extra_html: That changed in 2008, when the Supreme Court ruled in District of Columbia v. Heller that the amendment protects an individual right to keep arms in common use for lawful purposes such as self-defense in the home. Writing for SCOTUSblog, Alex Rivenbark explains that the harder question now is not whether the right exists but what counts as a protected "arm." Courts ask two things: is the item a "bearable arm," and is it "in common use" by ordinary law-abiding people? The right has always had limits — the Court has signaled that "dangerous and unusual" weapons, and those designed mainly for military use, may fall outside it. Those tests leave real disputes open, and lower courts have split over whether bans on semiautomatic rifles and large-capacity magazines are constitutional — questions the justices may yet have to settle. (This card describes U.S. constitutional law specifically.)

related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

flashcards.prompt: What did District of Columbia v. Heller (2008) establish about the Second Amendment?
flashcards.back_html: That it protects an individual right to keep arms in common use for lawful purposes like self-defense at home — not only a militia-related right.

flashcards.prompt: How do U.S. courts decide whether a weapon is a protected 'arm'?

choices.text: Whether it is a bearable arm and is 'in common use' by law-abiding people for lawful purposes
Whether the exact weapon existed when the amendment was written in 1791
Whether the local police department has approved it

flashcards.explanation_html: The Court's test asks if it's a bearable arm in common lawful use; "dangerous and unusual" or military-only weapons may fall outside protection.

flashcards.prompt: Which statement about the right to bear arms is accurate?

choices.text: It is not unlimited — 'dangerous and unusual' weapons can be restricted
It protects any weapon whatsoever, without exception
It applies only to people on active militia duty

flashcards.explanation_html: Even Heller recognized limits: the right covers common arms but leaves room to restrict dangerous and unusual ones.
